concepts.name: Repository
concepts.description: Storage location for your project and its history

types.name: Local Repository
types.description: Copy of the project on your local machine

types.name: Remote Repository
types.description: Hosted version of the project (e.g., GitHub, GitLab)

concepts.name: Working Directory
concepts.description: Local directory where you modify files

concepts.name: Commit
concepts.description: Snapshot of your project at a specific point in time

commands.name: git init
commands.description: Initialize a new Git repository

commands.name: git clone
commands.description: Create a copy of a remote repository

commands.name: git status
commands.description: Show which files are modified, staged or untracked

commands.name: git add
commands.description: Add files to staging area

commands.name: git commit
commands.description: Create a new commit with staged changes
commands.note: --amend replaces the previous commit, so avoid it once the commit has been pushed.

commands.name: git log
commands.description: Show the commit history of the current branch

commands.name: git restore
commands.description: Discard working-tree changes or unstage files (Git 2.23+)
commands.note: The modern replacement for the file-related uses of git checkout -- <file> and git reset HEAD <file>.

commands.name: git push
commands.description: Upload local commits to remote repository
options: -u (set the upstream branch on the first push)
--force-with-lease (rewrite the remote branch, but refuse if someone else pushed since your last fetch)
commands.note: After a rebase the branch must be force-pushed; prefer --force-with-lease over a bare --force.

commands.name: git fetch
commands.description: Download remote commits without merging them into your branch
commands.note: git pull is git fetch followed by git merge (or git rebase with --rebase).

commands.name: git pull
commands.description: Download and integrate remote changes

commands.name: git remote
commands.description: Manage the remote repositories a clone tracks

commands.name: git branch
commands.description: List, create, or delete branches
commands.note: -d refuses to delete a branch with unmerged commits; -D forces the delete.

commands.name: git switch
commands.description: Change the branch you are working on (Git 2.23+)
commands.note: The modern single-purpose alternative to git checkout for branches; git restore covers files.

commands.name: git checkout
commands.description: Switch branches or restore files
commands.note: Still valid, but git switch (branches) and git restore (files) are the modern equivalents.

commands.name: git merge
commands.description: Combine branches
options: --squash (bring the changes in as one uncommitted change set)
--abort (stop and restore the state before the merge)

commands.name: git rebase
commands.description: Reapply commits on top of another branch

workflows.name: Git Flow
workflows.description: A strict branching model for larger projects

workflows.name: Trunk-Based Development
workflows.description: Single main branch with short-lived feature branches
principles: Short-lived feature branches, typically merged within a day

operations.name: Cherry Pick
operations.description: Apply specific commits to current branch

commands.description: Save changes to stash
Apply and remove stashed changes
Apply stashed changes but keep the entry in the stash
List stashed changes
Delete every stashed entry

operations.name: git reset
operations.description: Move the current branch tip to another commit, rewriting local history
modes: --soft: moves the branch tip only; the changes stay staged
--mixed (default): moves the tip and unstages the changes; files keep their edits
--hard: moves the tip and discards changes in the staging area and working tree
operations.warning: Never reset a branch other people have pulled - it rewrites shared history. Use git revert instead.

operations.name: git revert
operations.description: Create a new commit that undoes an earlier commit, leaving history intact
operations.note: Safe on shared branches because it adds a commit instead of rewriting existing ones.

rows: Rewrites it - the commits leave the branch
Preserves it - adds an inverse commit
Unsafe - forces everyone else to recover
Local commits that were never pushed
Only the reverted changes are touched

operations.name: git reflog
operations.description: Log of every position HEAD has held, including commits no branch points at any more
operations.note: The standard way to recover work lost to a bad reset, rebase or branch delete.
operations.warning: Reflog entries are local only and expire after about 90 days by default.

operations.name: git bisect
operations.description: Binary search through history to find the commit that introduced a bug
operations.note: Git checks out a midpoint commit each round; mark it good or bad until the first bad commit is found.

operations.name: git tag
operations.description: Mark a specific commit, normally a release
operations.note: Annotated tags (-a) store an author, date and message; tags are not pushed by default.

solution: git status to identify conflicting files
Complete merge with git commit (or git merge --continue)
git merge --abort to back out and restore the pre-merge state
git revert <commit-hash> if the commit is already pushed - never reset a shared branch
git log to copy the hash of the misplaced commit
Back on the wrong branch, git reset --hard HEAD~1 - only if the commit was never pushed
If it was already pushed, git revert <commit-hash> on the wrong branch instead
git reflog to find the hash HEAD pointed at before the mistake
git reset --hard HEAD@{n} to move the branch back
Or git checkout <hash> then git switch -c recovery to rescue it onto a new branch
